content:
Tom Cruise has spent years as one of the few stars whose name alone could fill a theater. This month, theaters are filling with someone else — because exhibitors just pulled his movie from 2,535 of them in a single weekend.

"Digger," Cruise's $160-to-$180 million dark comedy from Oscar winner Alejandro G. Iñárritu, has cratered so completely that Warner Bros. removed it from roughly 76% of its screens heading into its third weekend — the 10th-biggest single-weekend theater-count drop ever recorded, alongside disasters like "The Rhythm Section" and "Cry Macho." That's the headline. Here's everything verified so far.

The numbers

"Digger" opened Oct. 2, 2026 in 3,321 North American theaters with just $8 million domestic — Cruise's lowest opening as a leading man in 19 years, trailing only 2007's "Lions for Lambs" ($6.7 million). Another $12 million overseas brought the global debut to roughly $20 million. Week two fell 60% to $3.2 million. The third weekend collapsed 71% to about $920,000 from only 786 theaters.

The running totals: $17.2 million domestic, $24.5 million international, $41.7 million worldwide. Industry sources project the film will finish near $50 million globally — against production costs of $160–$180 million plus roughly $100 million in marketing. Variety and TheWrap sources put the projected theatrical loss at $245–$250 million, knocking on the door of "John Carter's" record. Audiences gave it a C+ CinemaScore; Rotten Tomatoes sits at 53%.

The film

Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, a billionaire oil tycoon attempting to convince the world he can save humanity from the catastrophe his own drilling caused — a dark satire co-written by Iñárritu with Sabina Berman, Alexander Dinelaris Jr. and Nicolás Giacobone. The ensemble includes Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons and Emma D'Arcy.

Warner Bros. reportedly spent $100 million marketing the film, ran a "Decide for Yourself" campaign to push audiences past the reviews, and had famous friends — Anne Hathaway, Ben Affleck, Jane Fonda, Guillermo del Toro, Glen Powell, Michael Mann, Ron Howard — championing it on social media. None of it moved the needle.

Cruise's take

Cruise is taking the long view. He said last week that he "never thought of movies when I'm making them (in terms of) opening weekend" and prioritizes making films that "will translate, last and evolve."

Why this one matters

Black comedies at this budget simply don't exist for a reason, and there's something almost admirable about the biggest star alive spending his post-"Maverick" capital on an Iñárritu art film instead of another franchise entry. But the exhibitors have spoken, and losing more than two thousand screens in one weekend is about as clear a signal as this industry sends. Divisive swings do sometimes get reassessed — "Birdman" wasn't exactly a box office phenomenon either — but that kind of reevaluation takes years. For now, the verdict is financial, not artistic: a $250 million hole in the balance sheet, opened just as Warner Bros.' Paramount Skydance merger closes.
